passage: Mohit lined up the medals in his head: cricket for Rehan, drawing for Tia, chess for Kabir. And him? Nothing. He said it out loud in the lift to Sudha Aunty from the third floor. "I'm not special at anything." She pressed the button for the ground floor. "You're ten, Mohit. Nobody is finished at ten. Come to my Saturday club and just try things." On Saturday his clay bowl leaned like a tired tower. He laughed, hands full of grey clay, and Sudha Aunty laughed too. Later he tried the drum, badly, and loved the noise. In the lift on the way home he was thinking about next Saturday, not about medals.

qa.q: Where did Mohit tell Sudha Aunty that he was not special at anything?
qa.a: He said it in the lift.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he lined up his friends' medals and found nothing for himself?
qa.a: He felt insecure and ordinary, as if everyone else had something and he had nothing.

qa.q: What small step helped Mohit?
qa.a: Going to Sudha Aunty's Saturday club and trying different things, enjoying them without needing to be the best.

qa.q: How might Sudha Aunty see Mohit's worry?
qa.a: As common at his age. She sees a child still early in finding what he likes, so she invites him to try things instead of compete.

grounding: Shows a child certain he has no special talent who finds enjoyment in trying different things.

passage: Rain hammered the roof, so the whole Class 4 was stuck indoors for break, and the room was a roar of voices. Pradeep Sir, hurrying to finish the notice for assembly, asked, "Siddharth, read this out for me?" Siddharth read it, his voice steady over the noise. Pradeep Sir stopped writing. "You pause at the commas. Even the back row heard you. Did you know that?" Siddharth blinked. "No, Sir." "That is a real skill. Take this storybook home and read a page aloud each day." Siddharth held the book with both hands. He felt taller, though he couldn't say why.

qa.q: Why was the class stuck indoors?
qa.a: Rain hammered the roof, so they could not go out for break.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when Pradeep Sir praised his reading?
qa.a: Surprise, and a feeling of being seen. He had not known he had that skill, and he felt taller afterwards.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do to keep growing this skill?
qa.a: He can keep reading a page of the storybook aloud each day, perhaps to someone at home who can tell him how it sounds.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep Sir have spoken up in the middle of all that noise?
qa.a: He noticed something real and wanted Siddharth to hear it, since one honest word of encouragement can open a path. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a small reading skill a child never saw, giving honest encouragement and a way to keep practising.

passage: "You came home quiet today, Vikas. Sit, I'll tell you something. I'm Deepak, your Dada, and I was ten once, in Kanpur. A boy named Suraj started calling me Kaalu because my skin was dark. Every day, in front of everyone. It cut me. I began walking the long way to school so I wouldn't pass him. One evening I told my mother, hardly able to get the words out. She held my face and said his words told her about him, not me. Next day she came with me and spoke to my teacher. And there was Bhola, who shared his marbles and never asked why I was sad. So. What happened at school today?"

qa.q: What did Suraj call Deepak?
qa.a: He called him Kaalu, because Deepak's skin was dark.

qa.q: How did the teasing make young Deepak feel, and how can you tell?
qa.a: It hurt him deeply. He said it cut him, and he walked the long way to school to avoid Suraj.

qa.q: What could Vikas do now, and who might help?
qa.a: He can tell a trusted adult such as his Dada what happened and stay close to kind friends. 🤍

qa.q: How might Dada see Vikas coming home quiet?
qa.a: As a sign Vikas is hurting. Dada remembers that feeling, so he shares his own story gently instead of pushing.

grounding: Shows an elder remembering being teased about skin colour, telling a trusted adult, and finding a kind friend.

passage:
Tuesday, 9 pm. Hated the mirror today. My ears stick out and my tummy looks odd in the school shirt. I wanted to stay in the bathroom forever.

Then football at the park. I ran the whole length of the ground and scored, and my legs did that. Strange, they didn't feel ugly then.

Told Usha Masi at dinner. I could hardly get the words out. She didn't laugh. She said lots of children feel like this, she did too at my age, and we can talk any time. Tomorrow we're going to the park together.

Still don't love the mirror. A bit lighter, though.

- Vishal

qa.q: What did Vishal do on the football ground?
qa.a: He ran the whole length of the ground and scored.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling as he looked in the mirror?
qa.a: Shame and dislike about how he looked. He wanted to stay in the bathroom forever.

qa.q: What helped Vishal feel a bit lighter?
qa.a: He remembered what his legs did at football and told Usha Masi, an adult he trusts, how he felt.

qa.q: How might Usha Masi see Vishal telling her?
qa.a: She was probably glad he trusted her, and she understood because she felt the same at his age. She listened without laughing. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child disliking his reflection, noticing what his legs can do, and telling a trusted adult.

passage: Ingrid sat cross-legged in front of the TV in Porto as an advert for face cream ended. The girls in it were thin, pale and glowing. In the dark screen she saw her own reflection, freckled arms and all. "I don't look like that," she said quietly. Her cousin Rafael, who edits pictures for a small magazine, looked up from his laptop. "Come here." He opened a photo of a model and dragged some sliders. The skin went smooth, the waist thinner, the colour lighter. "That's how it's made. Nobody looks like that, not even her." Ingrid looked at the screen, then at her arm. "Real people look all sorts of ways, tall, round, dark, pale," he said. "Watch the people on the tram tomorrow."

qa.q: What does Rafael do for work?
qa.a: He edits pictures for a small magazine.

qa.q: Why did Ingrid say quietly, "I don't look like that"?
qa.a: She was comparing herself with the girls in the advert and beginning to feel she wasn't good enough.

qa.q: What could Ingrid do next time an advert makes her feel that way?
qa.a: She can remember that pictures are edited and look at the real people around her, who look all sorts of ways. 🙂

qa.q: How might Rafael see Ingrid's remark?
qa.a: He knows how much editing goes into such pictures, so he probably felt concerned and wanted to show her what is behind them.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling not good enough beside edited media images and learning that images are edited and real people vary.

passage: Note from Salma, school counsellor. Kiran, Class 6, came to see me after lunch. She told me that at breakfast her father said she was beautiful exactly as she is. She rolled her eyes: "Papa has to say that." I asked what she thought about it. She said she doesn't believe it, but she keeps hearing it anyway. I noticed she was picking at the end of her plait and had avoided the mirror by the door. What I did: I told her she doesn't have to believe it today, and that hearing it often may still matter. We agreed to talk again next week.

qa.q: What did Kiran say about her father's words at breakfast?
qa.a: She said, "Papa has to say that."

qa.q: What does Kiran's admission that she keeps hearing her father's words suggest she is thinking?
qa.a: She doubts it about herself, yet the words have stayed with her, so a part of her may want to believe them.

qa.q: How could Salma support Kiran next?
qa.a: She can keep checking in without pushing Kiran to believe it yet, and encourage her father to keep showing steady warmth.

qa.q: How might Kiran's father feel when she brushes off his words?
qa.a: He may be hurt or worried, but he likely means them and will keep saying them, and that steady love is what she can build on.

grounding: Shows a parent's unconditional statement about how a child looks, disbelieved yet remembered, seen by a counsellor.

passage: During the school's PT period, Jyoti kept tugging at her uneven fringe, which she had trimmed herself the night before. Rehana Ma'am blew the whistle. "Pair up for kho-kho!" Imran ran across the ground. "Jyoti, you're my partner. Team B is going down!" He never glanced at her hair. In the second round she stopped tugging; by the third she was laughing and out of breath, her fringe stuck to her forehead. Rehana Ma'am, watching from the shade, noticed Jyoti's shoulders had come down from around her ears. Imran only wanted someone quick to chase with. When the bell rang, Jyoti had forgotten all about her hair.

qa.q: Which game did Imran choose for the pair?
qa.a: They played kho-kho.

qa.q: How can you tell that Jyoti felt relaxed with Imran?
qa.a: She stopped tugging at her fringe in the second round, was laughing by the third, and her shoulders came down.

qa.q: What might Jyoti take from this?
qa.a: That some friends care about playing together, not how she looks, and she can seek them out when she feels self-conscious.

qa.q: How does Imran see the moment?
qa.a: He only wanted a quick partner to beat Team B and did not even glance at her hair, so to him she was simply a good teammate.

grounding: Shows a friend who ignores how she looks and only wants to play, leaving her relaxed.

passage: Rain had turned the track to slush an hour before the final, and Dhruv's shoes squelched at the start line. The whistle went. Mud flicked up his calves, his lungs burned, and he leaned at the tape a stride ahead. First place. He threw both arms up, laughing, legs trembling and happy. Manoj wheeled over from the fence, palms dark with mud from his wheels. "That last stretch was wild!" "Thanks!" Dhruv said. "Your shot in Saturday's basketball match made the whole gym go quiet. Will you teach me the bounce pass?" Manoj grinned. "Only if you can keep up with the chair."

qa.q: What had made the track slushy?
qa.a: Rain had turned the track to slush an hour before the final.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling after crossing the tape first?
qa.a: Joy and pride in what his body had just done. He threw both arms up, laughing.

qa.q: How does Dhruv show respect for Manoj's body and skill?
qa.a: He praises Manoj's shot and asks to be taught the bounce pass, valuing what Manoj's body can do.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Dhruv's request?
qa.a: Probably as welcome, because it treats him as someone with skill to share rather than someone to pity.

grounding: Shows joyful pride in a race win alongside respect for a classmate whose body works differently.

passage:
Wednesday night. Irawati Aaji went to the temple and left the laddoo box open on the table. I'm allowed one. I took one. Then I looked at the door, and nobody was there. My hand actually went out for a second. Then I pulled it back. I don't know why, just that I'd know. Later I folded all the clothes from the line, properly, even the small socks, instead of making a pile and saying I was tired. When Aaji came home she didn't count anything or check anything. She just asked about my day. I felt light. I like the me who did that. 🙂

- Sarika

qa.q: How many laddoos was Sarika allowed?
qa.a: She is allowed one.

qa.q: Why did Sarika pull her hand back from the box?
qa.a: She knew she would know, so she wanted to be someone she can trust even when nobody is watching.

qa.q: What did Sarika's choices give her, and what could she remember if the urge returns?
qa.a: They gave her a light feeling and trust in herself. If the urge returns she can remember that feeling and do her chore first.

qa.q: How might Irawati Aaji see Sarika's honesty?
qa.a: She never counted or checked, so she probably simply trusts Sarika and is happy to hear about her day.

grounding: Shows a child with nobody watching who refrains from taking an extra sweet and does her chore honestly.

passage: Ten minutes were left in the maths test when the teacher was called to the office, leaving the answer key open on the front desk. Tanvir's heart thudded. Three sums were still blank and the clock seemed loud. Damini, at the next desk, glanced at the key, then at him, and raised her eyebrows. That morning on the bus he had decided: if the chance ever comes, I get up and go to the water jug. So he stood, walked to the back for a drink, legs shaky, and stayed there a moment. When he sat down he stared at the third sum until a method came, even if the answer might be wrong. The teacher returned as the bell rang.

qa.q: What was left open on the front desk?
qa.a: The answer key was left open on the front desk.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling as the teacher left the room?
qa.a: Tension and temptation. His heart thudded, and three sums were still blank.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's plan from the bus work better than fighting the urge on the spot?
qa.a: He had already decided what to do, so he only had to follow the plan and walk to the water jug.

qa.q: What might Damini have been thinking when she raised her eyebrows?
qa.a: Perhaps she was tempted too or curious what Tanvir would do. Her look might be an invitation, but we can't be sure.

grounding: Shows a child tempted by an open answer key who follows a decision made beforehand and walks away.
